newsitem.title: USA: Kodak profits fall 14 percent, stock tumbles.
newsitem.headline: Kodak profits fall 14 percent, stock tumbles.

text.p: Eastman Kodak Co. said on Wednesday its second-quarter profits fell 14 percent, hurt by the strong U.S. dollar, growing losses for digital products, higher marketing expenses and price competition.

The surprisingly poor results dragged down the film maker's stock. Kodak tumbled $8.75, or more than 11 percent, to $68.125 in afternoon trading on the New York Stock Exchange, where it was the most actively traded issue.

"These unsatisfactory results reflect continuing problems executing some of our business plans, as well as the very significant impact of adverse foreign exchange and an intensifying competitive environment," said George Fisher, Kodak's chief executive.

"These factors, plus the continuing heavy investment in aggressive marketing of our Advantix products and strategic investments in our digital products and services, will make it very difficult to grow 1997 operating earnings per share beyond the 1996 level."
The Advantix brand of cameras, which was introduced last year, allows users to select different photo sizes when taking a picture.
Kodak Chief Financial Officer Harry Kavetas later said in an interview that the company could cut some U.S. film prices by 5 percent or more this year.
"We have no interest in losing market share. We'll take that kind of action if we have to," Kavetas said when asked whether price cuts would occur this year.

How much the company will cut prices depends "a lot on what the other players do, including our competitors," Kavetas said. The reductions could exceed 5 percent by year's end, depending on the product, he added.
Kodak's earnings slid to $368 million, or $1.12 per share, from $440 million, or $1.30 per share, in the year-ago period. Analysts had expected earnings of $1.39 per share.
Sales fell 6 percent to $3.9 billion from $4.1 billion after the company sold the marketing, service, and facilities management operations of its Office Imaging business last year.

"We continue to take the long view, investing for growth, particularly in Advantix, emerging markets and digital products, while managing our core consumer business both for share growth and market expansion," Fisher said.
"Although we will sustain these investments, we have concluded that all company units will accelerate their ongoing cost reduction programmes."

After adjusting for Office Imaging, U.S. sales edged up 2 percent, while foreign sales were essentially flat, including the effects of currency exchange rates. Results from emerging markets generally improved during the second quarter, posting double-digit sales growth.

Despite growing losses from digital products, Fisher said Kodak remains committed to expanding the product line through internal development and alliances. The products include scanners, printers, films, writeable CDs and software.

Consumer imaging segment sales for the second quarter rose 5 percent to $2.121 billion, reflecting strong growth in revenue from services, particularly photofinishing operations. However, earnings from operations fell 16 percent to $353 million as competition grew, Kodak continued aggressive marketing efforts to support the Advantix system and the dollar strengthened.
Sales for the commercial imaging segment fell 2 percent to $1.739 billion, while earnings slid 6 percent to $197 million.

Strong performance by entertainment imaging was offset by continuing weakness in the Rochester, N.Y.-based company's traditional micrographics business, as well as digital, graphic arts and certain medical products, it said.
Kodak said it will be difficult to grow 1997 operating earnings per share beyond the 1996 level.
Over the long term, Kodak said it remains committed to increasing earnings per share by an average of at least 10 percent per year.
